findings.title: Validator increments block statistics on every validation, including the email-only check
findings.body: EmailValidator calls BlockedEmail.should_block?(value), which is a side-effecting method that increments match_count and last_match_at and saves the record. Every time a User is validated (including repeated validations on save, or validations that later fail for other reasons), the counter is bumped. The statistics become meaningless and every validation performs a write.

findings.title: should_block? mixes a query with a write and ignores save failures
findings.body: should_block? writes match_count and last_match_at as a side effect of a predicate-named method, using record.save with no check of the result, and without an atomic increment. Concurrent calls lose increments (read-modify-write race), and the method name hides the write. A failed save (e.g. validation on the record) is silently ignored.

findings.title: Email lookup is case-sensitive while users' emails are normalized
findings.body: BlockedEmail.where(email: email) compares the raw string. User emails are downcased via Email.downcase elsewhere in the codebase, and the blocked_emails table stores whatever was entered. An entry 'Bad@Spam.com' will not block 'bad@spam.com', so blocking is trivially bypassed.

findings.title: Blocked-email check is applied to any attribute using the validator
findings.body: The validator is generic (ActiveModel::EachValidator) but the blocked-email lookup runs unconditionally, and the error key is hardcoded to user.email.blocked. Any future use on other attributes will apply the block list and misreport. Also the not_allowed/blocked messages are added to attribute, fine, but the check is coupled to User semantics.

findings.title: Returning user attributes and raw errors in the create response leaks data
findings.body: The failure response now includes values from user.attributes.slice('name','username','email') and the full errors hash. This echoes submitted data back and exposes validation detail (including the blocked-email signal) to unauthenticated callers, which lets anonymous users probe whether an email is blocked via the 'is not allowed.' error, bypassing the generic message.

findings.title: rejectedEmails is populated from result.values.email, which may be undefined
findings.body: pushObject(result.values.email) is guarded only by result.values being truthy. If the server omits email (e.g. the field is absent), undefined is pushed, and the email check then never matches the real address. The entry is also never removed, so a user who corrects a typo stays blocked only for the rejected string, but a legitimately fixed email is still validated correctly; the main issue is the undefined push and unbounded growth of the array.

findings.title: Unique index without a case-normalized value and no email format constraint
findings.body: The unique index on email is case-sensitive, so the same address in different cases can be stored twice, and only one of them would be matched by the case-sensitive lookup. Normalization should happen at write time or in the index expression.

findings.title: Validator spec does not test the whitelist/blacklist behavior it moved
findings.body: The User email_validator and email_in_restriction_setting? logic was moved into EmailValidator, but the new spec only covers blocked emails. Regressions in the whitelist/blacklist domain checks are not caught. The spec also stubs should_block? so the side-effect bug above is never exercised.

findings.title: No test for uniqueness, case handling, or save failure
findings.body: The spec does not verify the uniqueness validation or case-insensitive matching, and does not verify that validation (not just should_block?) leaves match_count unchanged. The 'updates statistics' expectation passes while the validator incorrectly increments counts on each User validation.
